content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Across all four blind responses the settled reading is that the dog is a strongly negative symbol of uncleanness, contempt, and moral impurity, denoting persons outside or hostile to the holy community — the wicked generally, Gentiles/outsiders (esp. Matt 15/Mark 7), false teachers (Phil 3:2), apostates (2 Pet 2:22), and violent enemies/scavengers of judgment (Ps 22; 1 Kgs 21). No single narrow referent dominates every passage.","book_summary":"The book defines the dog as a wild beast representing a kingdom or its citizens — especially Rome in the crucifixion pattern. Gentile 'dogs' eat crumbs from Israel's table (Matt 15/Mark 7), and the dogs that 'compassed' the sufferer in Psalm 22:16 are identified with the Roman soldiers surrounding Jesus at the cross (Matt 27).","consensus_core_identification":"Dog = unclean, contemptible persons excluded from or hostile to the covenant/holy community (wicked, Gentiles, false teachers, apostates, persecuting enemies), with the referent varying by context.","book_core_identification":"Dog = a Gentile kingdom or its citizens, paradigmatically Rome, whose soldiers fulfill the 'dogs' of Psalm 22 at the crucifixion.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book narrows the consensus's broad class of unclean/contemptible outsiders to a corporate-political referent: a specific kingdom (Rome) and its Gentile citizens. It drops or ignores consensus cases such as false teachers (Phil 3:2), apostates returning to vomit (2 Pet 2:22), and the wicked generally, and it reclassifies the dogs of Psalm 22:16 from generic violent enemies/persecutors to Roman soldiers specifically. Revelation 22:15's 'dogs' would likewise shift from the immoral/wicked generally to citizens of the Gentile kingdom.","material_contradiction":"","rationale":"The consensus already lists 'Gentiles or people outside Israel's covenant' as a common referent (Matt 15:26-27; Mark 7:27-28), so the book's central identification remains within a recognized consensus category rather than replacing it. What the book changes is the boundary and precision: it makes the corporate-political sense (kingdom/citizens, especially Rome) the primary meaning, applies typological reclassification to Psalm 22:16 via Matthew 27, and excludes several consensus applications (false teachers, apostates, general wickedness). This is a material boundary disagreement without contradiction of the negative Gentile-outsider core, fitting REFINED.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue DIVERGENT because 'a kingdom or its citizens' is a categorically different kind of referent (a political entity) than the consensus's moral/ritual class of unclean persons, and no consensus response identifies dogs with Rome or any kingdom; the Psalm 22–Matthew 27 link is a novel typological move not present in any blind response. However, since the Gentile-outsider referent is explicitly listed as common in consensus and the book builds on it, narrowing rather than replacement is the better description.","confidence":"medium"}
